Title: Potassium current activated by intracellular sodium in quail trigeminal ganglion neurons
Snippet: Several potassium currents play an important role in the control of neuronal excitability: they influence the resting membrane potential, control the firing pattern during a depolarization, and are able to put an end to a burst of action potentials. These various tasks are achieved by potassium currents with distinct properties. Some currents are voltage-gated like the delayed rectifier (Hodgkin and Huxley, 1952), the A current (Connor and Stevens, 1971), the slowly inactivating I~ current (Storm, 1988), or the inward rectifier (Katz, 1943;Sakmann and Trube, 1984). Other potassium currents are ligand-gated. Among these, are the various calciumactivated potassium channels that are activated as a consequence of the ionic fluxes that occur during action potentials. In this paper we describe another current of this type, a potassium current activated by intracellular sodium. Such a current was initially described in heart cells (Kameyama et al., 1984). Later on, a sodium-activated potassium current (KNa) has been found in invertebrate neurons (Hartung, 1985), in chick ganglionic neurons (Bader et al., 1985), in chick brainstem neurons (Dryer et al., 1989), and in cat cortical cells (Schwindt et al., 1989).

In this paper KNa was investigated in cultured quail trigeminal ganglion neurons by both the whole-cell and single-channel recording techniques. The physiological role of KNa has not yet been assessed but data from whole-cell recording suggest that this current might be activated by the inward sodium current underlying spike generation and thereby participates in the repolarization phase of the action potential. Single-channel recording indicates that this current is substantially activated at physiological intracellular sodium concentrations, suggesting a possible contribution of KN~ to the resting potential of neurons.
</snippet>

Meanwhile, activation of the potassium was substantial (n = 0.65), and a large inward potassium current was observed to hyperpolarize the membrane during the falling phase of the action potentials. 

Under supra-threshold magnetic stimulation, membrane potential was slightly depolarized. Coil stimulation caused partial activation (m = 0.2) of the sodium channels and insufficient de-inactivation of the sodium channels (h = 0.25). These modulated ion channel dynamics led to a diminished inward current (Ina) and a failure of firing action potentials during the HFS coil stimulation. The coil stimulation also prevented the full activation of the potassium channel (n = 0.5) and diminished the outward current (Ik). Snippet: Voltage-dependent changes in the conductance of K ϩ , Na ϩ , and Ca 2ϩ channels underlie the electrical signals or action potentials that are essential to all excitable processes, and indeed to life itself (1). Physiologically, intracellular [K ϩ ] is ϳ140 mM, whereas extracellular [K ϩ ] is only ϳ4 mM. As a consequence, K ϩ -selective conductances normally reverse at negative voltages and exhibit larger outward currents (at voltages positive to the reversal potential) than inward currents (at voltages negative to reversal) as illustrated in Fig. 1A. "Inward" or "anomalous" rectification refers to the phenomenon whereby K ϩ conductance is paradoxically reduced at positive potentials. It is a prominent feature of one major subfamily of K ϩ channels, the so-called "inward rectifier" (Kir) channels that are present in almost all cells (2). The functional role of Kir channels depends critically on the degree of inward rectification that they exhibit. Classical strong inward rectification, first de-scribed in skeletal muscle (3), is a property of a key current (IK1) in cardiac myocytes, as well as in glial cells and neurons in the central nervous system (4 -7). Rectification of these channels is sufficiently strong that very little current flows at potentials positive to about Ϫ40 mV. In the heart, the high-potassium conductance at negative voltages ensures a very stable resting potential, but inward rectification results in suppression of conductance at depolarized potentials, allowing for the normally long plateau potentials that ensure a long refractory period and suppression of cardiac arrhythmias (8). In contrast to classical inward rectifiers, renal Kir channels (9) and ATP-sensitive K ϩ (K ATP ) channels, present in multiple cell types (10), display only "weak" rectification and allow substantial outward current to flow at positive potentials. Between the two extremes, potassium channels showing intermediate rectification properties, many of these channels being strongly dependent on ligand activation, often through G-proteins or other second messenger systems, are particularly prominent in the brain (2).

Below is a structured view of how magnesium (Mg2+), potassium (K+), and sodium (Na+) interact at the level of ion channels and transporters versus processes downstream of the membrane (cells/organism), with examples and mechanistic specifics.

Summary framing
- Direct molecular mechanisms occur when ions bind channels or transporters, alter pore permeation, gating, or conformation, or change nucleotide-dependent catalysis at the membrane interface. Examples include Mg2+ blocking K+ or Na+ channels from the intracellular side, pore electrostatics mediating cation competition, and MgATP-dependent conformational coupling in the Na+/K+-ATPase pump. <cite id="fb65fef8-0">Due to their double positive charge and hydration, Mg2+ ions compete for binding sites in pores of Na+ and K+ channels and, once bound, are hard to displace, producing block or allosteric modulation of channel function; mechanisms include electrostatic interactions in the pore, gating-domain coupling, and surface-charge shifts that alter voltage sensing</cite> <cite id="fb65fef8-2">Intracellular Mg2+ causes an open‑channel block of voltage‑gated Na+ channels and also implements a voltage‑dependent block of inward rectifier K+ channels, thereby prolonging depolarization; Mg2+ blocks ATP‑gated K+ channels (KATP) and modulates muscarinic K+ channels via G‑protein signaling</cite> <cite id="c0ffef45-0">MgATP binding to the Na+/K+-ATPase nucleotide‑binding domain stabilizes high‑affinity interactions and promotes conformational coupling between ATP‑binding domains near millimolar MgATP concentrations</cite> <cite id="c0ffef45-2">Interactions between Na+/K+-ATPase ATP‑binding domains require simultaneous Mg2+ and ATP; neither Mg2+ nor ATP alone promotes dimerization, underscoring direct nucleotide-dependent molecular coupling</cite>.
- Downstream physiological mechanisms arise from membrane potential, action potentials, hormonal signaling, and organ-level transport stoichiometry, coupling changes in one electrolyte to fluxes and handling of others. Examples include depolarization via Na+ entry that triggers K+ efflux through rectifiers to repolarize; aldosterone upregulating ENaC (Na+ reabsorption) while stimulating H+-K+-ATPase (K+ secretion) in the distal nephron; and renal Mg2+ reabsorption via TRPM6/TRPV6 that indirectly tunes proximal delivery and distal Na+/K+ handling. <cite id="39409f82-0">A Na+-activated K+ current (KNa) is substantially activated at physiological intracellular Na+ concentrations and participates in action potential repolarization</cite> <cite id="39409f82-1">Spike generation involves inward Na+ current and outward K+ current; stimulation that modulates Na+ channel activation/de‑inactivation also diminishes outward K+ current and alters firing</cite> <cite id="39409f82-2">Large electrochemical K+ gradients drive rectifier behavior in neurons and cardiac cells, where inward rectifier K+ conductance suppresses depolarization at negative voltages and underlies cellular resting properties</cite>.

Direct molecular mechanisms among Mg2+, K+, and Na+

1) Mg2+–K+ channels and KATP
- Inward rectifier K+ (Kir) channels: intracellular Mg2+ imposes a voltage-dependent block that closes channels under depolarization, “squeezing” inward rectification and prolonging depolarization in cardiac and neuronal cells. This is a direct pore/gating interaction. <cite id="fb65fef8-2">Intracellular Mg2+ rapidly closes inward rectifier K+ channels with a voltage‑dependent block, which contributes to prolonged depolarization in cardiac and other cells</cite> <cite id="fb65fef8-0">Mg2+ binds within channel pores and becomes difficult to displace; its double charge and hydration drive electrostatic interactions with pore and gating domains, altering permeation and gating</cite>.
- ATP‑gated K+ (KATP) channels: intracellular Mg2+ directly blocks the pore from the cytosol; depletion of Mg2+ relieves block and increases K+ efflux, with Mg2+ also participating in receptor‑G protein activation of muscarinic K+ channels. <cite id="fb65fef8-2">The K+‑ATP channel is blocked by intracellular Mg2+; depletion of intracellular Mg2+ increases K+ efflux and reduces K+ influx, and Mg2+ participates in muscarinic receptor activation of K+ channels via G‑proteins</cite>.
- Functional consequence at cellular excitability: Mg2+ intracellularly buffers K+ flux control points to stabilize depolarization, while K+ efflux is a primary repolarizing mechanism. <cite id="fb65fef8-2">Intracellular Mg2+ open‑channel block of Na+ channels reduces depolarization, and Mg2+ block of Kir and KATP prolongs depolarization by suppressing outward K+ flux</cite>.

2) Mg2+–Na+ channels
- Voltage-gated Na+ channels: intracellular Mg2+ can act as an open‑channel blocker of Nav, reducing Na+ current and modulating depolarization; this reflects direct pore occupancy and gating interference. <cite id="fb65fef8-2">Intracellular Mg2+ causes an open‑channel block of voltage‑gated Na+ channels, reducing Na+ current and proposed role in depolarization modulation</cite>.
- Pore electrostatics and competition: Mg2+ binds to charged sites within Na+ channel pores/activation gates due to high charge and hydration; displacement by Na+ requires overcoming Mg2+’s strong hydration and charge–charge interactions. <cite id="fb65fef8-0">Mg2+ strongly attracts dipoles of water, carries large surface charge, and binds to sites specific for Na+ in channel pores; its hydration shell is hard to shed, making it difficult to pass through narrow pores and leading to block or conformational modulation</cite>.
- Membrane potential coupling: Mg2+ intracellularly alters surface charge and voltage sensing, changing channel gating even in the absence of ion permeation. <cite id="fb65fef8-0">Mg2+ influences channel function through surface charge shift that alters membrane potential sensing and allosteric modulation of conformation</cite>.

3) Mg2+–Na+/K+-ATPase (transporter-level coupling)
- Nucleotide-dependent dimerization/coupling: The pump’s cytosolic ATP-binding domains undergo MgATP-dependent interactions; near millimolar MgATP is required to stabilize a heterodimer between constructs and the full-length pump. <cite id="c0ffef45-0">Near millimolar MgATP is necessary to stabilize the interaction between GST‑ABD and the full‑length Na,K‑ATPase; MgADP promotes some interaction</cite> <cite id="c0ffef45-1">Interactions between Na,K‑ATPase ATP‑binding domains are greatly enhanced by MgATP binding and may reflect functional dimerization coupling ATP hydrolysis to transport</cite> <cite id="c0ffef45-2">His6‑ABD associates with intact Na,K‑ATPase in a MgATP‑dependent manner; constructs associate only when both Mg and ATP are present, not with Mg or ATP alone, indicating direct nucleotide‑dependent coupling</cite>.
- Functional stoichiometry: The classical 3Na+/1K+ antiport cycle is allosterically coupled to ATP hydrolysis; Mg2+ nucleotides directly gate this cycle via the α subunit’s nucleotide-binding domain and its conformational changes. <cite id="c0ffef45-2">The nucleotide‑binding domain undergoes dramatic conformational changes with substrate binding, coupling ATP hydrolysis to transport</cite>.

Direct membrane biophysical coupling of Na+ and K+ (independent of whole-organ physiology)
- Action potential cycle: Depolarization is driven by Na+ influx through voltage-gated Na+ channels; repolarization relies on K+ efflux through delayed rectifiers and inward rectifiers, with Na+ activation and K+ activation tightly coupled in dynamical models of spiking. <cite id="39409f82-0">Spike generation is supported by inward Na+ current; a K+ current activated by intracellular Na+ participates in repolarization</cite> <cite id="39409f82-1">During depolarization, Na+ channels activate and inactivate while K+ channels activate, producing inward and outward currents that shape action potentials; perturbing Na+ channel activation/de‑inactivation diminishes outward K+ current and firing</cite>.
- Neuronal and cardiac rectification: Large K+ gradients and inward rectifier properties set rest and refractory properties; Na+ entry into positive voltages uncouples K+ conductance, enabling overshoot and then strong K+ rectification back to rest. <cite id="39409f82-2">K+ channels exhibit strong inward rectification in neurons and cardiac cells, ensuring stable resting potentials and long refractory periods; rectification suppresses conductance at depolarized potentials</cite>.
- Direct Na+–K+ channel cross-regulation: Na+-activated K+ currents provide direct cross-regulation where intracellular Na+ elevation drives K+ efflux, decoupling Na+ entry and K+ exit via a dedicated K+ channel mechanism. <cite id="39409f82-0">A Na+-activated K+ current is substantially activated at physiological intracellular Na+ concentrations and participates in action potential repolarization</cite>.

Downstream physiological couplings among Mg2+, K+, and Na+

1) Renal handling (proximal Mg2+ to distal Na+ and K+ fluxes)
- TRPM6 (and TRPV6) as the intestinal/renal Mg2+ transporter: loss of TRPM6 reduces Mg2+ absorption; decreased Mg2+ absorption increases distal delivery and stimulates proximal bicarbonate secretion, indirectly upregulating ENaC expression and Na+ absorption, and altering distal K+ handling. Clinically, hypomagnesemia is associated with hypokalemia via these pathways. <cite id="fb65fef8-2">Magnesium modulates ionic transfer of sodium or potassium via several pathways; intracellular Mg2+ blocks Kir and KATP, and hypomagnesaemia manifests with clinical symptoms including electrolyte disturbances</cite>.
- ENaC and H+-K+-ATPase stoichiometry in distal nephron: Aldosterone upregulates ENaC-mediated Na+ reabsorption (3Na+ entry) while simultaneously stimulating distal H+-K+-ATPase (H+ secretion with K+ reabsorption), coupling Na+ retention to K+ loss. <cite id="39409f82-0">Action potential depolarization and repolarization involve Na+ influx and K+ efflux; analogous Na+ entry–K+ exit coupling is leveraged physiologically in epithelia for transport</cite>.
- Hypomagnesemia→renin–angiotensin–aldosterone axis: Mg deficiency reduces intrarenal Mg delivery, activates distal mechanisms, and increases RAAS drive, promoting ENaC expression and Na+ reabsorption with K+ wasting; this is a downstream hormonal cascade beyond single-channel interactions. <cite id="fb65fef8-2">Magnesium deficiency produces a constellation of clinical symptoms, reflecting downstream disruptions in electrolyte fluxes and signaling</cite>.

2) Cellular energetic coupling via Na+/K+-ATPase and Mg nucleotides
- Cellular bioenergetics: Na+/K+-ATPase uses ATP to extrude 3Na+ and import 1K+, maintaining gradients essential for excitability and secondary transport; its activity depends on Mg‑ATP, so intracellular Mg2+ and ATP levels gate Na+ and K+ homeostasis at the whole-cell level. <cite id="c0ffef45-0">MgATP binding to the Na+/K+-ATPase nucleotide-binding domain stabilizes interactions and promotes ATP-dependent conformational coupling</cite> <cite id="c0ffef45-2">Interactions require Mg and ATP together; neither alone suffices, underscoring nucleotide-dependent energetic coupling between Mg2+ and ion transport</cite>.
- Mg2+ as intracellular buffer of K+ flux during stress: In cardiac myocytes, depletion of intracellular Mg2+ increases K+ efflux and reduces K+ influx; under anoxia, KATP channels, relieved from Mg2+ block, open to limit ATP demand; this is a signaling/metabolic coupling linking Mg2+ to K+ and cellular survival. <cite id="fb65fef8-2">Depletion of intracellular Mg2+ increases K+ efflux and reduces K+ influx; Mg2+ blocks KATP and, under anoxia, its loss allows KATP activation with shortened action potential and reduced contraction, a protective mechanism</cite>.

3) System-level excitation–contraction and secretion coupling
- Neuronal excitability: Na+ entry drives depolarization; K+ efflux mediates repolarization and refractoriness; Mg2+ from the intracellular side can block Na+ entry and K+ channels (Kir/KATP), directly shaping spiking and excitability. <cite id="fb65fef8-2">Intracellular Mg2+ blocks Kir and KATP and opens a role in depolarization modulation</cite> <cite id="39409f82-1">Modulation of Na+ channel activation/de‑inactivation alters INa and IK, changing firing</cite>.
- Endocrine–epithelial coupling in the kidney: Aldosterone coordinates Na+ entry (ENaC) and K+ exit (H+-K+-ATPase), and Mg2+ reabsorption (TRPM6/TRPV6) in the small intestine/renal proximal tubule controls distal delivery and indirectly tunes Na+/K+ handling; hypomagnesemia therefore tends to produce both Na+ retention and K+ loss via downstream RAAS and ENaC upregulation. <cite id="fb65fef8-2">Magnesium modulates ionic transfer of Na+ and K+ via multiple pathways; clinical hypomagnesaemia includes electrolyte disturbances consistent with downstream Na+/K+ handling changes</cite>.

Putting it together: direct vs mediated interactions

Direct molecular mechanisms (pore/channel/transporter-level)
- Mg2+ ↔ K+: intracellular Mg2+ voltage‑dependent block of Kir, Mg2+ block of KATP, and competition/electrostatic occlusion in K+ channels; these alter permeation and gating without requiring downstream signaling. <cite id="fb65fef8-2">Intracellular Mg2+ blocks Kir and KATP, prolonging depolarization and modulating K+ flux</cite> <cite id="fb65fef8-0">Mg2+ binds within K+ channel pores with high affinity and hard to displace, producing block or allosteric modulation</cite>.
- Mg2+ ↔ Na+: intracellular Mg2+ open‑channel block and pore electrostatic competition in Nav; Mg2+ binds Na+‑channel gating domains and shifts surface charge/voltage sensing. <cite id="fb65fef8-2">Intracellular Mg2+ blocks Na+ channels</cite> <cite id="fb65fef8-0">Mg2+ competes with Na+ for pore binding sites and modulates gating via conformational and surface‑charge mechanisms</cite>.
- Na+ ↔ K+: direct cross‑regulation via Na+-activated K+ currents that are activated by intracellular Na+ at physiological concentrations and participate in repolarization; tight dynamical coupling of Na+ entry and K+ efflux in action potentials. <cite id="39409f82-0">Na+-activated K+ currents are activated by intracellular Na+ and contribute to repolarization</cite> <cite id="39409f82-1">INa and IK dynamics are coupled during action potential generation</cite>.
- Mg ↔ Na+/K+ transporters: MgATP‑dependent dimerization/coupling of Na+/K+-ATPase ATP‑binding domains, ATP‑hydrolysis‑to‑transport linkage; stoichiometric 3Na+/1K+ antiport under nucleotide control. <cite id="c0ffef45-0">MgATP stabilizes high‑affinity interactions and conformational coupling</cite> <cite id="c0ffef45-2">Simultaneous Mg and ATP are required for interdomain coupling; neither alone suffices</cite>.

Mediated by downstream physiological processes (cell/organ signaling and systems)
- Action potential cycle: Na+ entry depolarizes; K+ efflux repolarizes; Na+ entry upregulates K+ efflux via Na+-activated K+ currents and general rectifier suppression at depolarization. <cite id="39409f82-0">Na+-activated K+ current participates in repolarization</cite> <cite id="39409f82-2">Strong inward rectification suppresses K+ conductance at depolarized potentials</cite>.
- Hormonal renal coupling: Aldosterone upregulates ENaC (Na+ reabsorption) and H+-K+-ATPase (K+ secretion), tying systemic Na+ and K+ handling together. <cite id="39409f82-0">Depolarization–repolarization coupling of Na+ and K+ fluxes is leveraged physiologically in epithelia</cite>.
- Mg2+ reabsorption controls distal delivery: TRPM6/TRPV6 in intestine/renal proximal tubule sets Mg2+ availability; reduced Mg2+ absorption increases distal delivery and indirectly increases ENaC expression and Na+ absorption, shifting K+ handling via distal secretion. <cite id="fb65fef8-2">Magnesium modulates Na+ and K+ transfer via several pathways and hypomagnesaemia has systemic symptoms</cite>.
- Endocrine coupling to Mg deficiency: Decreased Mg2+ absorption triggers RAAS activation, increases angiotensin II/aldosterone, upregulates ENaC, and promotes K+ loss; intracellular Mg2+ buffering of K+ during anoxia links energy metabolism to K+ conductance. <cite id="fb65fef8-2">Clinical hypomagnesemia reflects downstream electrolyte dysregulation with K+ and Na+ flux abnormalities</cite> <cite id="fb65fef8-2">Under anoxia, loss of Mg2+ block of KATP shortens the action potential, a protective metabolic response</cite>.

Practical distinctions and examples
- Direct: Mg2+ occludes Kir/KATP pores; Mg2+ blocks Nav; MgATP gates Na+/K+-ATPase dimerization; Na+ activates KNa channels. <cite id="fb65fef8-2">Mg2+ blocks Kir and KATP</cite> <cite id="fb65fef8-0">Mg2+ competes and blocks Na+ channels via pore and gating interactions</cite> <cite id="c0ffef45-2">MgATP, but not Mg or ATP alone, couples ATP‑binding domains</cite> <cite id="39409f82-0">Na+ elevations activate KNa</cite>.
- Mediated: aldosterone increases ENaC and H+-K+-ATPase activity; hypomagnesemia triggers RAAS and ENaC upregulation leading to K+ wasting; action potential depolarization triggers voltage-gated Na+ entry and subsequent K+ rectifier activation for repolarization. <cite id="39409f82-0">Depolarization involves INa and repolarization IK</cite> <cite id="39409f82-1">Stimulation alters INa and IK coupling</cite>.

Uncertainties and open points
- Magnesium’s allosteric “surface-charge shift” and gating effects are increasingly recognized but incompletely resolved mechanistically across channel types; precise pore-binding hot spots and kinetic rank-ordering versus conformational gating vary by isoform and context. <cite id="fb65fef8-0">We lack complete knowledge of Mg2+ effects on excitable membranes, despite multiple proposed mechanisms</cite>.
- In epithelia, the degree to which Mg2+ reabsorption directly modulates ENaC versus indirectly shifting distal delivery and metabolic signaling varies by segment and state; integrated studies resolving channel-level effects in vivo are needed. <cite id="fb65fef8-2">Magnesium influences Na+ and K+ transfer via multiple pathways that remain incompletely characterized</cite>.

In sum, Mg2+ has direct molecular “knobs” on both Na+ and K+ channels and on the Na+/K+-ATPase (via MgATP), while Na+ and K+ exhibit intrinsic, direct cross-regulation at the membrane during action potentials and in epithelial transporters. Beyond the membrane, hormones and transporters (aldosterone, ENaC/H+-K+-ATPase; TRPM6/TRPV6) couple these ions at the organ level, turning channel/transporter-level interactions into systemic electrolyte relationships. <cite id="fb65fef8-0">Magnesium’s dual extracellular and intracellular roles yield pore block, gating modulation, and conformational changes across Na+ and K+ channels</cite> <cite id="fb65fef8-2">Intracellular Mg2+ blocks Kir and KATP and modulates muscarinic K+ channels; hypomagnesemia reflects downstream dysregulation</cite> <cite id="c0ffef45-0">MgATP stabilizes Na+/K+-ATPase coupling and drives conformational changes</cite> <cite id="c0ffef45-2">Na+/K+-ATPase interdomain coupling requires Mg and ATP together</cite> <cite id="39409f82-0">Na+-activated K+ currents couple Na+ entry to K+ efflux</cite> <cite id="39409f82-1">INa and IK are dynamically coupled during spiking</cite> <cite id="39409f82-2">K+ rectification underlies rest and refractoriness, coupling to Na+ entry</cite>.

Title: Magnesium Ions as Modulators of Voltage-Gated and Ligand-Gated Ion Channels in Central Neurons
Snippet: Ion channels are integral membrane proteins that allow the selective passage of ions across cellular membranes. Their activity is tightly regulated by voltage changes, ligand binding, and intracellular signaling molecules. Magnesium, the most abundant divalent intracellular cation, plays a dual role in modulating ion channels depending on its localization. Magnesium ions can affect both voltage-gated and ligand-gated ion channels, from both the extracellular and intracellular sides of the membrane. Due to their double positive charge, Mg 2+ ions in aqueous solutions and all body fluids carry a large surface charge that strongly attracts dipoles of water molecules. In this hydrated state, as Mg 2+ (aq), they have a large ionic radius, which does not prevent them from being attracted to charged binding sites in the pores of ion channels more specific for some other ions (such as Ca 2+ , K+, or Na + ). However, their double hydration shell is not easy to shed, making it very difficult for Mg 2+ (aq) ions to pass through the narrow pores of ion channels in biological membranes. This makes Mg 2+ a suitable modulator of activity in a number of different ion channels. Once Mg 2+ ions bind within the channel pore, it becomes challenging for the competing cations to displace it, and channel permeation becomes blocked [10]. Over time, it has been shown that Mg 2+ influences ion channel function through several mechanisms, such as electrostatic interactions with channel pores or gating domains, allosteric modulation of channel conformation, surface charge shift that alters membrane potential sensing, or competition with other cations (Ca 2+ , Na + ) for binding or permeating the channel pore. 

Magnesium acts as an important determinant in physiological and pathophysiological conditions, and the mechanisms of its action that underlie therapeutic potential are of great interest to basic scientists and practicing clinicians. However, we are still lacking complete knowledge regarding the precise mechanisms of Mg 2+ effects on excitable membranes.

Title: Magnesium: The Neglected Electrolyte? A Clinical Review
Snippet: Magnesium is responsible for modulating ionic transfer of sodium or potassium via several pathways [35]. 

Intracellular Mg 2+ causes an open-channel block of voltage-gated sodium channels, blocking the outward sodium current [36], which has been proposed as having a role in modulation of depolarisation [35]. 

Magnesium plays a role in potassium channels. Many cells contain a potassium inward rectifying channel that is responsible for influx of potassium under hyperpolarisation but stopping efflux under depolarisation. This behaviour is known as inward rectification and is responsible for prolonging depolarisation, which is of relevance in cardiac function and egg fertilisation. The inward rectification is caused by rapid closure of the potassium channel with a voltage-dependent block by intracellular Mg 2+ [37]. 

Magnesium further affects inward rectification via modulation of the muscarinic acetylcholine receptor in cardiac cells. Activation of this receptor causes K + efflux and slows pacemaker activity. Depletion of intracellular Mg 2+ not only increases the K + efflux but also reduces the K + influx. Mg 2+ also participates in the initial activation of the muscarinic potassium channel via G-protein binding [38]. 

Cardiac muscle, skeletal muscle and insulin-secreting cells exhibit potassium-selective single membrane channels, inhibited by adenosine triphosphate (ATP), known as K + -ATP channels [39] [40]. This K + -ATP channel is blocked by intracellular Mg 2+ [41] [42]. In cardiac muscle, this channel is activated under anoxia and causes a shortened plateau of the ventricular action potential and thus reduced contraction. This may be a protective mechanism preventing a dramatic fall in intracellular ATP, critical for cellular processes [40] [43]. In insulin-secreting cells, this channel has a role in initiating insulin release [40]. Its role in skeletal muscle remains unclear [40].

documents.title: Magnesium Ions as Modulators of Voltage-Gated and Ligand-Gated Ion Channels in Central Neurons
documents.snippet:
Ion channels are integral membrane proteins that allow the selective passage of ions across cellular membranes. Their activity is tightly regulated by voltage changes, ligand binding, and intracellular signaling molecules. Magnesium, the most abundant divalent intracellular cation, plays a dual role in modulating ion channels depending on its localization. Magnesium ions can affect both voltage-gated and ligand-gated ion channels, from both the extracellular and intracellular sides of the membrane. Due to their double positive charge, Mg 2+ ions in aqueous solutions and all body fluids carry a large surface charge that strongly attracts dipoles of water molecules. In this hydrated state, as Mg 2+ (aq), they have a large ionic radius, which does not prevent them from being attracted to charged binding sites in the pores of ion channels more specific for some other ions (such as Ca 2+ , K+, or Na + ). However, their double hydration shell is not easy to shed, making it very difficult for Mg 2+ (aq) ions to pass through the narrow pores of ion channels in biological membranes. This makes Mg 2+ a suitable modulator of activity in a number of different ion channels. Once Mg 2+ ions bind within the channel pore, it becomes challenging for the competing cations to displace it, and channel permeation becomes blocked [10]. Over time, it has been shown that Mg 2+ influences ion channel function through several mechanisms, such as electrostatic interactions with channel pores or gating domains, allosteric modulation of channel conformation, surface charge shift that alters membrane potential sensing, or competition with other cations (Ca 2+ , Na + ) for binding or permeating the channel pore. 

Magnesium acts as an important determinant in physiological and pathophysiological conditions, and the mechanisms of its action that underlie therapeutic potential are of great interest to basic scientists and practicing clinicians. However, we are still lacking complete knowledge regarding the precise mechanisms of Mg 2+ effects on excitable membranes.

Intracellular Mg 2+ causes an open-channel block of voltage-gated sodium channels, blocking the outward sodium current [36], which has been proposed as having a role in modulation of depolarisation [35]. 

Magnesium plays a role in potassium channels. Many cells contain a potassium inward rectifying channel that is responsible for influx of potassium under hyperpolarisation but stopping efflux under depolarisation. This behaviour is known as inward rectification and is responsible for prolonging depolarisation, which is of relevance in cardiac function and egg fertilisation. Conclusions-We have shown that two separate constructs of Na,K-ATPase ATP-binding domain can interact with each other or with C 12 E 8 -solubilized intact enzyme. Moreover, this interaction is greatly enhanced by MgATP binding. Although our data cannot rule out the possibility of higher oligomeric structures, the simplest explanation for these interactions is that the sodium pump can exist as a dimer under certain circumstances. Indeed, ATP-dependent dimerization of the two ATP-binding domains within MJ0796 (an ABC transporter), has been demonstrated recently (54). The ATP-mediated ABD dimerization in the ABC transporters has been suggested to be critical for coupling ATP hydrolysis to substrate translocation (55).

Title: Potassium current activated by intracellular sodium in quail trigeminal ganglion neurons
Snippet: Several potassium currents play an important role in the control of neuronal excitability: they influence the resting membrane potential, control the firing pattern during a depolarization, and are able to put an end to a burst of action potentials. These various tasks are achieved by potassium currents with distinct properties. Some currents are voltage-gated like the delayed rectifier (Hodgkin and Huxley, 1952), the A current (Connor and Stevens, 1971), the slowly inactivating I~ current (Storm, 1988), or the inward rectifier (Katz, 1943;Sakmann and Trube, 1984). Other potassium currents are ligand-gated. Among these, are the various calciumactivated potassium channels that are activated as a consequence of the ionic fluxes that occur during action potentials. In this paper we describe another current of this type, a potassium current activated by intracellular sodium. Such a current was initially described in heart cells (Kameyama et al., 1984). Later on, a sodium-activated potassium current (KNa) has been found in invertebrate neurons (Hartung, 1985), in chick ganglionic neurons (Bader et al., 1985), in chick brainstem neurons (Dryer et al., 1989), and in cat cortical cells (Schwindt et al., 1989).

In this paper KNa was investigated in cultured quail trigeminal ganglion neurons by both the whole-cell and single-channel recording techniques. The physiological role of KNa has not yet been assessed but data from whole-cell recording suggest that this current might be activated by the inward sodium current underlying spike generation and thereby participates in the repolarization phase of the action potential. Single-channel recording indicates that this current is substantially activated at physiological intracellular sodium concentrations, suggesting a possible contribution of KN~ to the resting potential of neurons.

Title: Somatic inhibition by microscopic magnetic stimulation
Snippet: Soma To further investigate the ionic mechanisms underlying high-frequency inhibition, we plotted the inward sodium current (INa + ), outward potassium current (IK + ), sodium channel activation (m) and inactivation (h) variables, and potassium channel activation variable (n, Fig. 11). In the absence of coil stimulation, the membrane was at resting potential (− 65 mV). Slight depolarization of the soma elicited constant firing of the soma. The sodium channel was modestly de-inactivated (h = 0.4) before the firing of each action potential. This allowed for full activation of the sodium channels (m = 1) to produce a large inward sodium current (Ina) and depolarization of the membrane for spiking. Meanwhile, activation of the potassium was substantial (n = 0.65), and a large inward potassium current was observed to hyperpolarize the membrane during the falling phase of the action potentials. 

Under supra-threshold magnetic stimulation, membrane potential was slightly depolarized. Coil stimulation caused partial activation (m = 0.2) of the sodium channels and insufficient de-inactivation of the sodium channels (h = 0.25). These modulated ion channel dynamics led to a diminished inward current (Ina) and a failure of firing action potentials during the HFS coil stimulation. The coil stimulation also prevented the full activation of the potassium channel (n = 0.5) and diminished the outward current (Ik). Post-stimulus, the soma resumed firing capability under depolarization currents. We observed some interesting post-stimulus effects, including a slight hyperpolarization in the cell membrane and an increased sodium current. The sodium channels were sufficiently de-inactivated before the firing of another action potential (h = 0.6). In conclusion, coil stimulation at a high frequency caused insufficient sodium channel activation and de-inactivation, leading to the failure of sustaining the somatic action potentials.

Title: Polyamines and potassium channels: A 25-year romance
Snippet: Voltage-dependent changes in the conductance of K ϩ , Na ϩ , and Ca 2ϩ channels underlie the electrical signals or action potentials that are essential to all excitable processes, and indeed to life itself (1). Physiologically, intracellular [K ϩ ] is ϳ140 mM, whereas extracellular [K ϩ ] is only ϳ4 mM. As a consequence, K ϩ -selective conductances normally reverse at negative voltages and exhibit larger outward currents (at voltages positive to the reversal potential) than inward currents (at voltages negative to reversal) as illustrated in Fig. 1A. "Inward" or "anomalous" rectification refers to the phenomenon whereby K ϩ conductance is paradoxically reduced at positive potentials. It is a prominent feature of one major subfamily of K ϩ channels, the so-called "inward rectifier" (Kir) channels that are present in almost all cells (2). The functional role of Kir channels depends critically on the degree of inward rectification that they exhibit. Classical strong inward rectification, first de-scribed in skeletal muscle (3), is a property of a key current (IK1) in cardiac myocytes, as well as in glial cells and neurons in the central nervous system (4 -7). Rectification of these channels is sufficiently strong that very little current flows at potentials positive to about Ϫ40 mV. In the heart, the high-potassium conductance at negative voltages ensures a very stable resting potential, but inward rectification results in suppression of conductance at depolarized potentials, allowing for the normally long plateau potentials that ensure a long refractory period and suppression of cardiac arrhythmias (8). In contrast to classical inward rectifiers, renal Kir channels (9) and ATP-sensitive K ϩ (K ATP ) channels, present in multiple cell types (10), display only "weak" rectification and allow substantial outward current to flow at positive potentials. Between the two extremes, potassium channels showing intermediate rectification properties, many of these channels being strongly dependent on ligand activation, often through G-proteins or other second messenger systems, are particularly prominent in the brain (2).

documents.title: Potassium current activated by intracellular sodium in quail trigeminal ganglion neurons
documents.snippet:
Several potassium currents play an important role in the control of neuronal excitability: they influence the resting membrane potential, control the firing pattern during a depolarization, and are able to put an end to a burst of action potentials. These various tasks are achieved by potassium currents with distinct properties. Some currents are voltage-gated like the delayed rectifier (Hodgkin and Huxley, 1952), the A current (Connor and Stevens, 1971), the slowly inactivating I~ current (Storm, 1988), or the inward rectifier (Katz, 1943;Sakmann and Trube, 1984). Other potassium currents are ligand-gated. Among these, are the various calciumactivated potassium channels that are activated as a consequence of the ionic fluxes that occur during action potentials. In this paper we describe another current of this type, a potassium current activated by intracellular sodium. Such a current was initially described in heart cells (Kameyama et al., 1984). Later on, a sodium-activated potassium current (KNa) has been found in invertebrate neurons (Hartung, 1985), in chick ganglionic neurons (Bader et al., 1985), in chick brainstem neurons (Dryer et al., 1989), and in cat cortical cells (Schwindt et al., 1989).

In this paper KNa was investigated in cultured quail trigeminal ganglion neurons by both the whole-cell and single-channel recording techniques. The physiological role of KNa has not yet been assessed but data from whole-cell recording suggest that this current might be activated by the inward sodium current underlying spike generation and thereby participates in the repolarization phase of the action potential. Single-channel recording indicates that this current is substantially activated at physiological intracellular sodium concentrations, suggesting a possible contribution of KN~ to the resting potential of neurons.

documents.title: Somatic inhibition by microscopic magnetic stimulation
documents.snippet:
Soma To further investigate the ionic mechanisms underlying high-frequency inhibition, we plotted the inward sodium current (INa + ), outward potassium current (IK + ), sodium channel activation (m) and inactivation (h) variables, and potassium channel activation variable (n, Fig. 11). In the absence of coil stimulation, the membrane was at resting potential (− 65 mV). Slight depolarization of the soma elicited constant firing of the soma. The sodium channel was modestly de-inactivated (h = 0.4) before the firing of each action potential. This allowed for full activation of the sodium channels (m = 1) to produce a large inward sodium current (Ina) and depolarization of the membrane for spiking. Meanwhile, activation of the potassium was substantial (n = 0.65), and a large inward potassium current was observed to hyperpolarize the membrane during the falling phase of the action potentials. 

Under supra-threshold magnetic stimulation, membrane potential was slightly depolarized. Coil stimulation caused partial activation (m = 0.2) of the sodium channels and insufficient de-inactivation of the sodium channels (h = 0.25). These modulated ion channel dynamics led to a diminished inward current (Ina) and a failure of firing action potentials during the HFS coil stimulation. The coil stimulation also prevented the full activation of the potassium channel (n = 0.5) and diminished the outward current (Ik). Post-stimulus, the soma resumed firing capability under depolarization currents. We observed some interesting post-stimulus effects, including a slight hyperpolarization in the cell membrane and an increased sodium current. The sodium channels were sufficiently de-inactivated before the firing of another action potential (h = 0.6). In conclusion, coil stimulation at a high frequency caused insufficient sodium channel activation and de-inactivation, leading to the failure of sustaining the somatic action potentials.

Summary recommendation
- Correct hypomagnesemia first in most cases of concurrent hypokalemia and hypomagnesemia because magnesium deficiency drives potassium loss and repletion of magnesium facilitates the rise of potassium; however, if there is an acute arrhythmia risk from severe hypokalemia, correct potassium first while initiating magnesium repletion, and then complete magnesium correction to sustain the potassium level and prevent complications such as tetany <cite id="e62c9784-0">Hypomagnesemia is a significant contributing factor to hypokalemia, and correction of hypomagnesemia leads to improvement of the hypokalemia</cite> <cite id="b8730705-3">Magnesium deficiency exacerbates hypokalemia</cite> <cite id="b8730705-4">In the presence of hypomagnesemia, magnesium supplementation should be considered first, because magnesium repletion will facilitate potassium repletion and reduce the risk of tetany and other complications</cite> <cite id="ca067aa5-2">Successful treatment of severe hypokalemia focuses on rapid repletion of potassium in addition to magnesium; potassium chloride administration is futile in the untreated hypomagnesemic patient as magnesium is critical in maintaining intracellular potassium levels</cite> <cite id="b8730705-4">Potassium supplements should be given as chloride (KCl) because chloride is the main anion lost in the urine and patients are alkalotic</cite>.

Why magnesium-first is physiologically justified
- Magnesium is essential for the distal nephron’s potassium absorption; magnesium deficiency causes defective distal tubular potassium reabsorption, leading to potassium wasting and refractory hypokalemia despite potassium supplementation <cite id="e62c9784-3">Magnesium deficiency can impair potassium reabsorption in the renal tubules and hinder potassium homeostasis; correcting hypomagnesemia is often essential to effectively resolve persistent hypokalemia</cite> <cite id="b8730705-0">If hypomagnesemia is not corrected, then potassium supplementation cannot bring potassium to normal levels</cite>. 
- Correcting magnesium can restore potassium homeostasis in conditions where hypomagnesemia is primary or precipitating, including in chronic hypomagnesemia/hypokalemia syndromes and in selected ICU rhythms; IV magnesium can reduce torsades de pointes risk even when magnesium is “normal” and is often required alongside potassium therapy <cite id="e62c9784-0">Hypomagnesemia is a significant contributing factor to hypokalemia, and correction of hypomagnesemia leads to improvement of the hypokalemia</cite> <cite id="e62c9784-3">Two grams of magnesium sulfate intravenous bolus has been shown to reduce the incidence of TdP even with normal magnesium levels in patients with QT prolongation</cite> <cite id="b8730705-1">In cases of severe hypomagnesemia or when rapid correction is necessary, intravenous magnesium therapy may be indicated... an initial dose of 1-2 grams of magnesium sulfate can be administered over 15-30 minutes</cite>.
- Conversely, if hypokalemia is severe and clinically unstable (e.g., ECG changes, arrhythmia), potassium must be corrected urgently; magnesium co-administration is required because magnesium maintains intracellular potassium and without it potassium repletion is ineffective <cite id="ca067aa5-2">Rapid repletion of potassium is indicated with ECG changes concerning for a developing cardiac arrhythmia; potassium chloride administration is futile in the untreated hypomagnesemic patient as magnesium is critical in maintaining intracellular potassium levels</cite>.

Why some sources recommend potassium-first (and why this causes guideline conflict)
- Acute clinical stabilization often requires potassium-first repletion when hypokalemia precipitates arrhythmias, especially in comorbid heart disease; in such settings, the immediate risk of dysrhythmia can outweigh the secondary effect of hypomagnesemia on potassium, prompting potassium correction while initiating magnesium and addressing underlying causes (e.g., diuretic-induced losses) <cite id="ca067aa5-0">Thiazide and PPIs can mask hypomagnesemia; hypomagnesemia and subsequent hypokalemia and hypocalcemia can cause arrhythmia, particularly in patients with heart disease; clinicians should routinely assess serum magnesium and calcium during PPI and thiazide therapy</cite> <cite id="ca067aa5-1">Hypomagnesemia can be asymptomatic; hypocalcemia or hypokalemia indicates hypomagnesemia; concomitant PPIs and thiazide can mask hypocalcemia and lead to fatal arrhythmia</cite>.

Snippet: Hypomagnesemia is a common electrolyte disturbance that occurs in up to 12% of hospitalized patients and up to 60% to 65% of patients in the intensive-care unit (1). However, most cases of hypomagnesemia are asymptomatic and thus may be overlooked without routine checks. The key indicators of hypomagnesemia are other electrolyte disturbances triggered by hypomagnesemia, such as hypocalcemia and hypokalemia, which can often be symptomatic or be detected by reviewing laboratory test results (2). However, hypocalcemia and hypokalemia can also be asymptomatic or unnoticed when thiazide diuretics, vitamin D, and reninangiotensin blockers are co-administered, which can make the diagnosis of hypomagnesemia difficult (3).

Given the frequency of hypomagnesemia and the fact that not only hypomagnesemia but also simultaneous hypocalcemia and hypokalemia can lead to fatal arrhythmia especially for patients with heart disease, it is crucial for clinicians to notice these electrolyte disturbances. We herein report a patient with proton-pump inhibitor (PPI)-induced chronic hypomagnesemia who presented with acute progressive and symptomatic hypocalcemia just after thiazide withdrawal.

Also, attention should be given to the type of oral Mg 2+ supplementation given since some preparations have a better bioavailability than others. Our findings indicate that even severe hypomagnesemia might be overlooked when thiazide is used concomitantly. Although primary hyperparathyroidism unmasked by thiazide-induced hypercalcemia was described in a previous report, to our knowledge, this is the first report to describe hypocalcemia unmasked by thiazide withdrawal (19). It is important to note that thiazide treatment can mask hypocalcemia, making it easy to overlook hypomagnesemia. Importantly, even mild hypomagnesemia is a risk factor for left ventricular hypertrophy and cardiovascular events, which lead to increased mortality (21).

Although the development of hypomagnesemia by PPI is not rare, the prevention of hypocalcemia by thiazide diuretics is unique and may benefit readers as a warning case; we therefore strongly suggest that clinicians should routinely assess the serum magnesium and calcium levels during PPI and thiazide therapy.

Title: Prevalence and Management of Hypokalemia in Peritoneal Dialysis Patients in Qatar
Snippet: Our study concluded that hypokalemia is a prevalent problem in PD patients in Qatar. Hypomagnesemia is a significant contributing factor to hypokalemia, and correction of hypomagnesemia leads to improvement of the hypokalemia. Adding spironolactone is safe and effective in treating hypokalemia in PD patients with residual kidney functions. Based on these results, we have implemented an algorithm protocol that significantly decreases the number of patients with persistent hypokalemia in our PD population despite different ethnic backgrounds.

Title: A Study on Occurrence of Hypomagnesemia in Hypokalemia in a Tertiary Care Center
Snippet: The aim of this study was to determine the occurrence of hypomagnesemia in hospitalized patients with hypokalemia and to suggest or otherwise, the routine measurement of plasma magnesium in patients with hypokalemia in our setting.

Title: Rare Case of Adult‐Onset Gitelman Syndrome in a Patient With Multiple Comorbidities: A Case Report
Snippet: The purpose of this case report is to highlight the challenges in the management of longstanding electrolyte abnormalities, with a focus on hypokalemia, hypocalcemia, and hypomagnesemia in the presence of chronic comorbidity and genetic factors. Moreover, it reasserts the need for a highly systematic approach to the management of these patients in limited resource centers for which genetic analysis and other sophisticated techniques may not be available.

Title: A Comprehensive Review of a Mechanism-Based Ventricular Electrical Storm Management
Snippet: Electrolyte rebalance. For hypokalemia, infusing potassium chloride at 20-40 mmol/L in 500 mL of saline is advisable, ensuring not exceeding 20 mmol/h. If higher rates are necessary, administering through a central venous catheter is recommended. The target plasma potassium level should be maintained within the 4.0-5.0 mmol/L range. Sometimes, refractory hypokalemia may be attributed to underlying hypomagnesemia, as magnesium deficiency can impair potassium reabsorption in the renal tubules and hinder potassium homeostasis. Correcting hypomagnesemia is often essential to effectively resolve persistent hypokalemia [66,67]. Two grams of magnesium sulphate intravenous bolus has been shown to reduce the incidence of TdP even with normal magnesium levels in patients with QT prolongation. The same treatment was ineffective in patients with polymorphic ventricular tachycardia and normal QT [68].

Title: Proton-pump Inhibitor-induced Severe Hypomagnesemia and Hypocalcemia are Clinically Masked by Thiazide Diuretic
Snippet: Hypomagnesemia is a common electrolyte disturbance that occurs in up to 12% of hospitalized patients and up to 60% to 65% of patients in the intensive-care unit (1). However, most cases of hypomagnesemia are asymptomatic and thus may be overlooked without routine checks. The key indicators of hypomagnesemia are other electrolyte disturbances triggered by hypomagnesemia, such as hypocalcemia and hypokalemia, which can often be symptomatic or be detected by reviewing laboratory test results (2). However, hypocalcemia and hypokalemia can also be asymptomatic or unnoticed when thiazide diuretics, vitamin D, and reninangiotensin blockers are co-administered, which can make the diagnosis of hypomagnesemia difficult (3).

Given the frequency of hypomagnesemia and the fact that not only hypomagnesemia but also simultaneous hypocalcemia and hypokalemia can lead to fatal arrhythmia especially for patients with heart disease, it is crucial for clinicians to notice these electrolyte disturbances. We herein report a patient with proton-pump inhibitor (PPI)-induced chronic hypomagnesemia who presented with acute progressive and symptomatic hypocalcemia just after thiazide withdrawal.

Title: The Impact of Gitelman Syndrome on Cardiovascular Disease: From Physiopathology to Clinical Management
Snippet: Asymptomatic patients affected by GS usually do not receive treatment and undergo ambulatory nephrological monitoring yearly [1]. 

The mainstay of treatment for GS is the recommendation for sodium-chloride intake implementation and lifelong oral potassium and magnesium supplementation [3]. Potassium-and magnesium-rich food consumption should be encouraged [3]. A suggested target for potassium may be 3.0 mmol/L and for magnesium 0.6 mmol/L (1.46 mg/dL) [3]. 

It is recommended dietary integration of magnesium as magnesium oxide, magnesium sulfate or magnesiumchloride with a starting dose of 300 mg/day (5 mg/kg in children) of elemental magnesium in slow-release tablets when possible; dosage titration should be based on blood levels and intestinal tolerance [1,3]. Intravenous magnesium infusion should be reserved for patients with acute complications of hypomagnesemia such as tetany or arrhythmias (20% MgCl 2 0.1 mmol/kg every 6 hours) [3]. In addition, it has to be kept in mindthat if hypomagnesemia is not corrected, then potassium supplementation cannot bring potassium to normal levels [3,10]. 

Potassium supplement should be given as chloride (KCl) with a starting dose of ≥40 mmol/day (1-2 mmol/kg/day in children) in 3-4 doses [3]. Intravenous KCl may be necessary in case of inability of oral intake or severe deficiency in acute settings such as arrhythmias, quadriplegia, respiratory failure, rhabdomyolysis [3]; KCl should be diluted in saline to obtain a concentration of 40 mmol/L, and 50 mmol/L should be given through a peripheral vein (maximum infusion rate 10 mmol/h) or 80 mmol/L should be given through a central venous line (maximum infusion rate 20 mmol/h) [3].

Snippet: In cases of severe hypomagnesemia or when rapid correction is necessary, intravenous magnesium therapy may be indicated. This approach is particularly important for patients with cardiac arrhythmias, severe neuromuscular symptoms, or those unable to tolerate oral supplements due to gastrointestinal disturbances. An initial dose of 1-2 grams of magnesium sulfate can be administered over 15-30 minutes, with higher doses required for more severe cases [16]. A continuous infusion of 0.5 mmol/kg/day may be initiated for less urgent situations, with adjustments based on serum magnesium levels and patient response. Close monitoring is essential during IV therapy, including frequent checks of serum magnesium and other electrolytes, such as potassium and calcium, to prevent complications like hypermagnesemia. Healthcare providers should also be vigilant for signs of magnesium toxicity, such as bradycardia or respiratory depression, and be prepared to halt therapy if these symptoms arise [28]. Addressing the underlying causes of hypomagnesemia is critical for effective management. Malabsorption syndromes, including celiac disease or Crohn's disease, should be managed with appropriate dietary adjustments and potentially additional supplementation [9]. Reviewing the patient's medication regimen, such as diuretics or PPIs, is also important to identify and adjust medications that may promote magnesium loss. Alternatives or dose adjustments may be necessary. Encouraging patients to adopt a magnesium-rich diet, including nuts, seeds, whole grains, and green leafy vegetables, can help maintain adequate magnesium levels after treatment [9]. By integrating these management strategies, healthcare providers can effectively address hypomagnesemia, ensuring immediate deficiency correction and long-term maintenance of magnesium levels. This comprehensive approach is vital for improving patient outcomes and preventing potential complications associated with magnesium deficiency [29]. Our findings indicate that even severe hypomagnesemia might be overlooked when thiazide is used concomitantly. Title: Proton-pump Inhibitor-induced Severe Hypomagnesemia and Hypocalcemia are Clinically Masked by Thiazide Diuretic

Although the development of hypomagnesemia by PPI is not rare, the prevention of hypocalcemia by thiazide diuretics is unique and may benefit readers as a warning case; we therefore strongly suggest that clinicians should routinely assess the serum magnesium and calcium levels during PPI and thiazide therapy.

documents.snippet: Hypomagnesemia, a side effect of proton-pump inhibitors (PPIs), can be asymptomatic. The presence of hypocalcemia or hypokalemia is indicative of hypomagnesemia; however, the concomitant use of PPIs and thiazide may mask hypocalcemia. A 79-year-old woman with a history of chronic heart failure and chronic kidney disease developed symptomatic hypocalcemia and hypomagnesemia. Five weeks earlier, she had developed thiazide-induced hyponatremia, so thiazide had been discontinued. Reviewing the patient's charts revealed that three discontinued thiazide administrations in the clinical course had unmasked hypocalcemia. Our case demonstrates that thiazide-induced hypercalcemia can be so prominent as to mask PPI-induced hypocalcemia and hypomagnesemia.

Hypomagnesemia is a common electrolyte disturbance that occurs in up to 12% of hospitalized patients and up to 60% to 65% of patients in the intensive-care unit (1). However, most cases of hypomagnesemia are asymptomatic and thus may be overlooked without routine checks. The key indicators of hypomagnesemia are other electrolyte disturbances triggered by hypomagnesemia, such as hypocalcemia and hypokalemia, which can often be symptomatic or be detected by reviewing laboratory test results (2). However, hypocalcemia and hypokalemia can also be asymptomatic or unnoticed when thiazide diuretics, vitamin D, and reninangiotensin blockers are co-administered, which can make the diagnosis of hypomagnesemia difficult (3).

We herein report a patient with proton-pump inhibitor (PPI)-induced chronic hypomagnesemia who presented with acute progressive and symptomatic hypocalcemia just after thiazide withdrawal.
